title: Richard Vogel jumps to Rolex Grand Prix victory in Brussels
content:
Under pressure as the last rider to go at the Rolex Grand Prix in Brussels, Richard Vogel got into the zone.

Riding Gangster Montdesir into the vast grass arena at the Brussels Stephex Masters, the second-ranked German knew he had to produce something special after Brazilian Eduardo Pereira de Menezes had taken the lead with an error-free second round in a lightning-fast time.

Vogel pulled out all the stops until just before the end, when he slightly lowered his speed to let his French stallion take an extra stride between the last two obstacles. He ended up going clear, beating Pereira de Menezes by just over half a second to win the Rolex Grand Prix in Brussels. Vogel now has a chance to clinch the Rolex Grand Slam of Show Jumping when he competes at the CSIO Spruce Meadows “Masters” in Calgary, Alberta.

Fellow German Daniel Deusser finished third with Pepita Van T Meulenhof with four penalties.

“I knew I had to be very efficient everywhere and very quick,” Vogel told The Athletic. “I knew I really had to risk it all and try as much as I can. And thankfully Gangster was right with me. He jumped amazingly, and he’s a fast horse, so it was just enough, not by a lot, but just enough.”

Having won a team gold medal alongside Deusser at the world championships last week in Aachen, Germany, Vogel credited his team with getting Gangster ready for the final Rolex Series of the season.

“While I was in Aachen, Gangster was at home, so they did basically all the preparation leading up to Brussels,” Vogel said. “I only rode at home on Monday and Tuesday, and then we traveled here. So it’s really a big credit that goes to them having the horses in such good shape, training them at home, taking care of them 24/7,”  Vogel said.

With the victory in Brussels, Vogel turns his attention to the CSIO Spruce Meadows “Masters” held Sept. 9-13, where he will try to clinch the Rolex Grand Slam of Show Jumping with his top horse, United Touch S.

After back-to-back wins at the Dutch Masters in March and Aachen, Vogel is aiming to become only the second rider since Britain’s Scott Brash in 2015 to win three Rolex majors in a row.

Vogel won in Brussels after producing a double clear over two rounds in a demanding course designed by Olympic course designer Gregory Bodo.

“Brussels rewards whoever can hold their nerve through a deep field,” according to equestrian statistics agency Equiratings. And that’s exactly how it went.

Bodo’s course, set over 14 jumps of up to 1.60 meters to a tight time limit, pushed most riders to the limit. Only five competitors went clear in the opening round, with many stumbling over the final two obstacles.

Steve Guerdat was the man to beat entering Brussels as the newly crowned individual show jumping champion but left empty-handed after his mare Lancelotta dropped two rails.

The course stymied other top riders as Ben Maher, the reigning Olympic champion, Piergiorgio Bucci, a two-time Rolex Grand Prix winner this season, and three-time Brussels champion Niels Bruynseels were eliminated after finishing outside of the top 12.

Vogel praised Bodo for setting a fair course for both rider and horse.

“It was very doable,” Vogel said. “You never think, ‘Ooh, this is way too much or way too tough on the horses.’  It was a tough enough Grand Prix, but all horses, I think, even the ones with one or two down actually jumped right.”
